record_problems.argument:
All seven findings were checked against the primary texts on disk (archive.org enlarged-edition OCR `za3e.txt`/`ZeteticAstronomy-EarthNotaGlobe-3e-format2_djvu.txt`, Gutenberg 69892 for 1865, Gutenberg 55387 for Carpenter, two Dubay OCRs) rather than against the finding text, and all seven were substantially right. Four sub-claims inside them were wrong and were corrected rather than copied in, which is where most of the work went.

The two majors were the serious ones and both were the project's own convict-class defect pointed inward. (1) Section 5 called Carpenter's proof 32 "the cleanest single check on this page" because 6 ft at 3 miles reproduces sqrt(2Rh). It equally reproduces the zetetic tradition's own law: Parallax quotes Mayhew's Wonders of Science p. 357 at enlarged-ed. p. 160 — "when an object is removed from the eye 3000 times its own diameter, it will only just be distinguishable" — and adopts it ("The above may be called the law of perspective."). 3000 x 6 ft = 3.41 mi against the sphere's 3.00 mi, and the two laws cross at h = 2R/9e6 = 1.42 m, i.e. just under the six feet Carpenter names. The page was making its cleanest check at the one height where the rival predictions agree. Worse, the closing sentence said the perspective account "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever" — flatly contradicted three lines above in Carpenter's own proof 6 ("no matter how high we ascend above the level of the sea, the horizon rises on and still on as we rise"; Federal Hill, Baltimore, twenty-five miles) and in Rowbotham's proposition 2 and his "at a certain distance, less or greater, according to the elevation of the observer". Section 5 is rewritten: proof 32 demoted and explicitly labelled non-discriminating, proof 6 promoted, their law stated as linear in height against the sphere's square root, with the fifteen-thousand-mile figure and a non-circular check I added (their rule run backwards needs an eye only 352 ft up for a 200-mile horizon).

(2) Our headline internal-contradiction argument — his optics exempt the axis his own tilt-to-contact procedure uses — was published as an oversight of his while his printed answer to exactly that charge sat two sentences past the sentence we quote. He writes that the dip taken this way is the geometric angle "to which must be added the collimation", "always A, T, S, plus collimation", because "the spider's web of which the cross hair is made is placed in the actual centre; hence, in an observation, the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it". That is now in refutation 2(a), in the steelman's first reply, and in the gloss (which previously located his answer in the 1865 text only, telling a reader of the edition we quote that his reply lived elsewhere). The TLDR, which stated the exemption flat with no hedge at all, now says the defect acts off the axis and his procedure puts the horizon on it, "though he saw that objection and answered it in the same section" — and the weight is moved to the square-root scaling, which is what the body actually holds. The verdict survives: (c) never depended on (a), and demoting (a) from kill to pressure point strengthens rather than weakens the rejection of SELF-CONTRADICTED, so I updated both places that gave the rejection reasoning.

The four moderates were applied with corrections. The "10-to-17-mile ranges his text names" was a number in quotation-adjacent position that neither text carries (Experiment 7 says "a length of ten to twenty miles" and "Ten miles on each side"; Dubay 60 says "a clear, flat 10-20 miles"; the only "17 miles" in the enlarged edition is an Australian latitude discrepancy) — fixed to ten-to-twenty and 2.2-4.3 arcmin, in the refutation, in straw_man.detail where the same figure appeared, in the advocate's paraphrase of it, and in docstring note 5. The unscoped absence assertion about the 1849 pamphlet is now scoped and no longer waves away a 16-page text whose own title advertises sea-surface experiments. "A plane does not look like a bowl" is replaced with his actual theory of why a plane would look like a bowl — the amphitheatre/concavity passage two paragraphs before the balloon quotations and the long-room/tunnel analogy immediately after them. The collimation-definition problem in the reversal test is real and I fixed it, but not the way the finding proposed (see rejected). Docstring note 11(e) is a false report-up and is withdrawn in place.

Three further defects of the same classes turned up while verifying and were fixed: docstring note 2 had the two-face argument backwards ("[the residual] cannot reverse sign under transit" — it is precisely the residual that reverses); the gloss said Elliott "opens by conceding the point at issue" when he opens by saying the opposite and concedes in the next sentence, and it silently italicised "Philosophy imposes the truth upon us" in a quotation that carries no italics in the source; and a quoted phrase was truncated at "the several glasses" without an ellipsis, now quoted through "of the theodolite".

record_problems.argument: All six findings held up against the sources, so all six were applied; none was rejected. The two that mattered most were both cases of the project's own house offence pointed inward: a quoted string attributed to a source that does not contain it (the "nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" phrase is Andrew Young's, not the USNO's — I confirmed the USNO page verbatim, "obtained by adding the average apparent radius of the Sun (16 arcminutes) to the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)", and Young's page verbatim, "the sum of an average radius of 16 minutes, and a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes"), and a Dubay quotation stopped at the concession with the flat conclusion that finishes the same sentence dropped ("…unlike a hazy illusory mirage, and on a ball-Earth 25,000 miles in circumference should be 2,400 feet below the horizon", verified at flatearth.ws/eric-dubay). I recovered the Zetetic Astronomy pages through a reader proxy after sacred-texts.com returned Cloudflare interstitials to direct fetches, and established the page-marker convention from two of Rowbotham's own internal cross-references (za45 cites fig. 30 as "page 41" and it sits after the [p. 41] marker; za16 cites fig. 27 as "p. 39" and it sits before the [p. 40] marker) — so in this transcription the marker heads its page, and every page citation the entry makes (pp. 31, 32, 34, 35, 41, 272; EXPERIMENT 3 at p. 17, bounded by the last marker in za07 and the first in za09) checks out. Nothing here touches the verdict: the SELF-CONTRADICTED challenge rests on both items being on the one list, not on their distance apart, and the collimation magnitude survives every repairing of the comparison. One place I refined rather than followed the finding: finding 3's proposed replacement collapsed the comparison to two cases and would have discarded the EXPERIMENT 3 three-mile figure the entry already had right, so I kept three yardsticks and attached the factors separately (roughly 240 at six miles, roughly 250 at three, order a hundred against the "several feet" of the 1870 trial) rather than adopting its wording wholesale.

record_problems.argument:
All seven findings were checked against the primary texts before anything was edited; six were confirmed and applied in scripts/_b11_B10.py, and the seventh (the clusters.py record) is correct but sits outside the one file I own, so it goes to record_problems with an anchoring instruction rather than being applied.

The headline defect was real and was ours. Carpenter's proof 89 (Gutenberg #55387, lines 1342-1371 of the local carpenter100.txt) reads: "It is well known that the law regulating the apparent decrease in the size of objects ... is very different with luminous bodies ... Sail past the light of a small lamp in a row-boat on a dark night, and it will seem to be no smaller when a mile off than it was when close to it. Proctor says, in speaking of the Sun: 'his apparent size does not change,'--far off or near. And then he forgets the fact!" Carpenter asserts the law himself, in his own voice, with his own example, and endorses Proctor's line as "the fact". The entry's through-line - TLDR "the words are a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against", the §3 heading "is Proctor's sentence, borrowed", and compression.note "Nothing was misquoted; the speech act moved" - flattered our own provenance finding by relocating the movement's own claim onto an opponent, and it did so while our own source_wording field quoted "And then he forgets the fact!" unanalysed. force_upgraded ("a concession was re-used as a proof") cannot describe the Carpenter-to-list step, because proof 89 was already a numbered proof; the concession-to-proof move, if it happened anywhere, happened in 1885. Refiled as hedge_dropped, with the note saying openly that no enum value fits exactly and naming what the fragment actually strips: that the law is about how luminous bodies appear, that it is asserted to deny an inference, and that the paragraph ends by calling Proctor's objection a counterfeit rather than by reporting a measurement.

Three other confirmations. (a) Dubay #123 credits the 32-mile figure to "Flat-Earthers throughout the ages" and #147 cites nobody; the only naming of Zetetic Cosmogony located in the archive.org text of 200 Proofs is #31, which is the kite-flying/wind passage - matching the project doc's named-source map "Winship -> 31". "Documented at every link" was indefensible and is gone. (b) In the Winship scan, "We challenge the whole scientific world to disprove this statement," closes the sun's-DISTANCE argument at line 7812, immediately before the section heading "SUN'S DIAMETER." at 7816; the units error's own challenge is "Let him disprove this who can. If ever disproof is attempted, it will be a literary curiosity, well worth framing." at 7890-7896. The entry had the quote on the wrong claim while its own sources[] label placed it correctly - a self-contradiction inside one record. (c) The §6 "reverses it" was overstated and Rowbotham 1865 Section 8 supplies the defence: it already carries the whole mechanism ("as the air near the Earth is both more dense and more damp ... the light of the Sun must be dilated or enlarged as well as modified in colour") and only then subordinates it with "But the enlarged appearance ... is only an optical impression, as proved by actual measurement" plus Philips. 1881 chapter X keeps the identical mechanism ("the disc of light projected upon the atmosphere", verified via the served za28) and drops the concession, promoting the residue to "a striking argument against the rotundity of the earth". Recast as the edition diff, which is true, stronger, and survives the glare-versus-disc reply.

One incidental verification worth recording: I established the Winship scan's page-marker convention rather than assuming it, because the p. 120 citation is load-bearing (Scott 1901 gives the same page). The markers sit at the HEAD of their page - text following marker N is page N. Anchors: the contents list pages "Sun, The" 112, "Sun's Distance" 113, "Sun's Diameter" 119, "Stars, The" 120; the tightest test is the body heading "THE STARS" falling between markers 120 (line 7864) and 121 (line 7927), which the contents puts on 120. Under the foot convention it would be 121. So the sextant derivation is on printed p. 120 and the locator's "pp. 119-120" is correct as published.

The verdict is untouched and remains defensible. Nothing applied moves MISLEADING: finding 1 makes Carpenter's commitment to constancy stronger, not weaker, which if anything hardens the case against the fragment; the equal-size half still rests on an observation true in every model, and the constancy half is still true on one timescale and false on another.

record_problems.problem: clusters.py "B10" note: "Solar angular diameter in fact varies ~3.4% annually - the reason we have both total and annular eclipses" is wrong on the cause, and it renders as the basis line under the verdict chip. The Moon's disc runs 29'26" to 33'30" (a ~13.8% swing, nearly four times the Sun's 3.4%) and its mean disc is the smaller of the two - 31.07' against 31.97', computed from 2x1737.4/384400 and 2x695700/149598000 - so it is the Moon's distance variation that produces the two eclipse types. §1 of this entry publishes both figures, so the page currently disagrees with itself. Suggested replacement: "Coincidence of angular size is real and well known. The Moon's apparent diameter varies ~14% against the Sun's ~3.4%, and the Moon's mean disc is the smaller - which is why central eclipses are sometimes annular."

CONFIRMED AND FIXED. (1) The precedent cite was genuinely wrong: clusters.py:486-488 gives C09 the verdict UNFALSIFIABLE ("Devotional imagery is not survey data"), and scripts/_b9_C09.py:303 only *proposes* SELF-CONTRADICTED. Citing a pending proposal as settled precedent, in a rendered field, on a provenance page, is exactly the slip the finding names. (2) The ducting physics was wrong in our favour's opposite direction — k = 1/(1 + R dn/dh) goes to infinity at dN/dh = -157 N-units/km, so a duct is not "a larger k"; and the correct treatment (modified refractivity M = N + (h/R_e)x10^6 ~ N + 0.157h, with 0.157 per metre = 10^6/R) puts 1/R inside the very formalism used to compute ducted propagation on a flat grid, which is section 5's thesis arriving from the least convenient direction. Two sources added for it. (3) The bathymetry numbers really were two models chained as one: 1.0 m is 1% of depth (range scaling, no bending), 7.26 m is the pure-bending across-track shift holding depth, and the honest combined figure is about 3.5 m across-track and about 2.1 m in depth (about 1.9 m the other way for the opposite-sign bias). Each is now attached to its mechanism; the vertical term went UP, so the conclusion strengthens. (4) The unscoped SAR universal, the NWS label's two dropped hedges plus the grafted 60 nm figure (source wording verified by fetch: "often produces the largest errors, usually causing precipitation underestimation", and the 60 nm/124 nm POD drop belongs to a separate sentence attributing it to Kitchen and Jackson 1993).

REJECTED. Finding 2 asks us to demote the SELF-CONTRADICTED challenge to REFUTED on the ground that "one item whose named technique falsifies it" is not how this page uses the verdict. That is two branches, and both are in use. The intra-item branch is A19 (clusters.py:172-175), which has no originator, no source and no second item: the verdict rests entirely on the named instrument, "a gyrocompass finds true north by sensing Earth's rotation" - structurally identical to item 392's flat-earth phase. B06 is the same branch via the claimant's own source. The second half of the objection - that leaning on item 391 spends an item scored at R08 twice - fails on the legend's wording "another item on the same LIST", and on precedent: C10's counterpart is C03 and B13's is B07, both cross-cluster. Adopting the proposed fix would have replaced a correct verdict argument with one that mis-describes our own rubric - the same class of error the finding was aimed at. Instead the challenge now quotes the legend and names the precedents that actually exist.

record_problems.argument:
All five findings against D09 were checked against the primary files, not against the finding text, and all five turned out to name a real defect. Two of them I could do better than the proposed fix, and one of the proposed replacements would have introduced a fresh bibliographic error of exactly the class it was correcting.

Finding 1 (Kepler/Galileo) — CONFIRMED at source. I re-downloaded the exact djvu.txt the entry links (archive.org GalileoWasWrongTheChurchSungenisRobertA.Bennett4276, 1,771,293 bytes). "astrolog" returns exactly two hits: line 31273, "Without them Kepler would have been just another seventeenth-century astronomer struggling to make a living by reading astrological horoscopes" (the "them" being Brahe's charts and data), and line 31539, "Having previously dabbled in astrology, Galileo wrote a personal horoscope for Cosimo Medici". The entry described both as being about Galileo. Fixed in the gloss, in the sources[] label and in docstring note 4b, with the Kepler hit quoted so the error cannot be made again silently.

Finding 2 (unnamed scope of three searches) — CONFIRMED, and I widened the search rather than only narrowing the claim. The GWW file's own first page reads "Vol[ume] II / Chapters 7 to 13 / Seventh edition / ... 2013"; PG #69892's metadata and title page both give Simpkin, Marshall, 1865; PG #55387's title page gives "1885 ... 5th Edition: 6th Thousand". All three are now named in the gloss and in their labels. Beyond that, I located and searched the enlarged 1881 THIRD edition (archive.org zeteticastronomy-earthnotaglobe, file ZeteticAstronomy-EarthNotaGlobe-3e-format2_djvu.txt — title page "1881", and it carries the Sabine pendulum material that only the third edition has) and Dubay's 200 Proofs: "astrol", "zodia" and "horoscop" all return zero hits in both, as they do in the 1865 text and in Carpenter. So the zetetic-side absence is now established over four texts including the edition the movement actually circulates, not one.

Finding 3 (generalisation from three files to two lineages) — CONFIRMED. "Neither cosmological lineage brought this argument in" and docstring "The founding flat-earth texts have no astrology argument in them" are both unscoped absence claims. Both now read "in the texts searched", with what was NOT searched named in the body: Rowbotham's 1873 second edition, Volumes I and III of Galileo Was Wrong, and (in the docstring) Blount, Voliva, Johnson, Bouw, van der Kamp, Marshall Hall.

Finding 4 (leg 2 of the verdict challenge) — CONFIRMED on both counts. The punchline clause "and that occultist is a heliocentrist" is an attribution to Manly P. Hall, which the same paragraph says is not established, so "it needs no attribution at all" was false as written; and the defender's reply is decisive — D10's thesis is that heliocentrism has occult roots, so an occultist heliocentrist confirms D10 rather than contradicting it. "Either leg alone carries the verdict" and "needs no attribution at all" are struck; leg 2 is now explicitly "SUPPORTING ONLY" with both limits stated; refutation §5 restates the residue as an inconsistency of standing rather than a contradiction; the reply is added to advocate.best_defense as a fifth move and answered in preemptive (d), which records the concession and warns a later editor not to restore the struck sentences. survives stays at 4 and preemptive now carries four concrete changes, satisfying the deep.py rule that survives>=3 obligates a text change.

Finding 5 (three unsourced prevalence claims) — CONFIRMED. I re-read astro.com/swisseph/swephinfo_e.htm: it says the Swiss Ephemeris "is not a product for end users. It is a toolset for programmers to build into their astrological software" and that it "contains three ephemerides" — the JPL DE files, Astrodienst's compression, or Moshier's semi-analytic theory (based on DE404) — and it makes no adoption or market-share statement anywhere. All three prevalence claims are replaced by the documented version, which needs no market claim to make the same point, plus a standing instruction in note 8(d) not to reintroduce one. I also softened one further implicit prevalence claim in refutation §6 that the finding did not name.

The cluster verdict in clusters.py is untouched, as are all shared files.

record_problems.argument: All seven in-file findings against E15 checked against the primary sources and all seven applied; the eighth (clusters.py) is out of my ownership and is reported up with the proposed replacement text recorded in the entry docstring. Two of the findings were the kind this project exists to convict its subject of, and both were ours: the refutation told the reader that superconducting gravimeters see the free core nutation "with no astronomical input at all" (Rosat & Lambert in fact invert ETERNA-derived complex tidal gravimetric factors for the lunisolar diurnal waves Psi1/Phi1 against an astronomical tidal potential, ocean-loading-corrected with FES2004 — I read the HAL copy at /tmp/rosat.txt), and the gloss said the book's conclusion was "stated flatly and without qualification, and there is no hedge here to shelter behind" immediately before block-quoting a sentence that opens "Without this methodology". The second one was hardening the source's hedge in the source's rhetorical favour and against our own argument, since the antecedent is the three-source check that geodetic VLBI has performed since 1979 — the conclusion lapses on the book's own terms, which is a stronger answer than the one we were making. I verified the page numbers independently of the finding's leaf map (the only leaf→folio maps on disk are for the 2006 item, not the 7th edition): in /home/claude/g.txt the printed folio sits after that page's footnotes and before the next page's running head, so text following marker N is page N+1. That convention makes the entry's own pp. 205–206 VLBI locator correct and the other three citations one page low, exactly as the finding said. Nothing applied disturbs the MISLEADING verdict: the finding remains that the source's premises are false while its conclusion is conceded.

record_problems.argument:
All eight findings check out against the primary sources, and I applied all eight — but I rejected one clause of a proposed replacement (finding 2's "within minutes") because it reintroduced the same overclaim it was fixing, and I substituted the checked numbers instead.

Verification actually done, source by source:

WIEGERT ET AL., AJ 145:70 (2013), arXiv:1209.5980. Abstract: "The radiant at RA +18° and Dec +56° is typical of the `classical' Andromedids of the early 1800's, whose radiant was actually in Cassiopeia"; body: "the later showers (1850 onwards) and the storms of 1872/1885 had radiants of RA=+27°, Dec=+44°"; "The shower outburst occurred during 2011 Dec 3-5"; "primarily ejected during 3D/Biela's 1649 perihelion passage". Finding 4 CONFIRMED — our text had the paper saying the reverse of what it says. The 9°/12° offset in the proposed fix also checks out (18 vs 27, 56 vs 44), so I kept the numbers and gave both radiants explicitly rather than the word "displaced".

EGAL, WIEGERT, BROWN & VIDA, ApJ (2023), arXiv:2302.02915 + published PDF. "The main peak (ZHR ~27) occurred around 69°.42 ± 0°.01 (4 hr–4 hr 30 UT) on May 31"; "We find that ordinary cometary activity could have produced other TAH apparitions observed in the past, including in 1930 and 2017"; abstract opens "The τ-Herculids (IAU shower number #61 TAH)". Findings 2 and 5 both CONFIRMED.

YE & VAUBAILLON, MNRAS Letters 515:L45 (2022), full text at ar5iv: "Increased activity of the τ-Herculid meteor shower has been observed on 2022 May 30–31 but only reached ∼1/50 of storm level". Finding 2's rate point CONFIRMED; note the arXiv landing-page abstract is the revised one and does NOT carry this sentence — it is in the paper body, which is where I got it.

REJECTED CLAUSE. Finding 2's proposed replacement says the outburst arrived "within minutes of the 2001 and 2008 timings". It did not. Our own body gives Lüthen 04:55 UT and Horii 04:59 UT; Egal puts the observed main peak at 04h–04h30 UT. That is roughly 25–55 minutes, not "minutes". Writing "within minutes" would have been the same class of defect as the "rate and width in general agreement" clause it was replacing. I wrote "inside an hour of the times set down in 2001 and 2008" and gave the observed bracket, which is still a striking result for a 21-year-ahead forecast and is checkable.

SPURNÝ, BOROVIČKA, MUCKE & SVOREŇ, A&A 605:A68 (2017), full text at ar5iv: "Asher & Clube 1993 predicted that future encounters would occur in 1995, 1998, 2005, and 2008" and, separately, "Asher & Izumi 1998 showed that enhanced Taurid activity indeed occurred in the years when the center of the swarm was less than 40° in mean anomaly from the Earth". Finding 3 CONFIRMED: a 1998 paper cannot confirm 2005 and 2008, and our source label said it did. I also found an unflagged arithmetic slip in the same sentence: the paper says "The total number of Taurid fireballs recorded photographically ... in 2015 was about 200. This is much more than we recorded in any previous year" but "For this study we selected 144 Taurids with complete information about heliocentric orbits". The 113-member branch is a subset of the 144, not of the ~200; our body implied the latter. Fixed in the same edit and recorded in the docstring.

ROBERTSON, POKORNÝ, GRANVIK, WHEELER & RUMPF, PSJ 2:88 (2021): title is "Latitude Variation of Flux and Impact Angle of Asteroid Collisions with Earth and the Moon"; models the near-Earth OBJECT population; "the flux of impacts to the poles for Earth is 22% greater than the flux at the equator, and 55% greater for the Moon". Finding 6 CONFIRMED — the figure was being deployed in verdict_challenge against a claim about micrometeoroid fallout, a population the paper does not model. I scoped it in three places (body, verdict_challenge, source label) rather than two, so the transplant cannot recur from the label.

FINDING 1, the hedge/consistency defect, is the serious one and it is real. §2 opened "prediction is the one thing a coordinate relabelling cannot manufacture" and closed "They are not compatible with the Earth being somewhere else", while §5 says in our own voice that a Tychonic relabelling "reproduces ... every annual date". The entry's own advocate.preemptive forbids exactly that, and build.py strips the advocate block, so readers saw the violated sentence and not the instruction. Both sentences replaced with claims §5 can live with. This makes the entry MORE consistent with its STANDARD PHYSICS verdict ("real, already explained, does not discriminate"), not less, so the verdict is untouched and stands.

FINDING 8. I took the "cut it" branch rather than the "argue it" branch. The proposed argument — that a moving-sky model has no mechanism to impose the observer's 0.4 km/s on meteoroids already in the atmosphere — is not obviously sound and is uncited, and by the page's own logic in that same paragraph a relabelling that absorbs 29.8 km/s absorbs 0.46 km/s too. So the diurnal-aberration fact is retained, now cited, but explicitly marked as a fact about how the working model is assembled and NOT a further discriminator, with "this page does not claim it could not" stated in our own voice. §5 still lists exactly three survivors (the third is now the spherical-Earth/Tychonic-unavailability point alone), so no count moved. advocate.preemptive clause (2) rewritten to say TWO things carry the weight, not three, and to name the earlier draft's error so it is not reintroduced.

CITATION ADDED for the reduction chain: Peña-Asensio, Trigo-Rodríguez, Gritsevich & Rimola, MNRAS 504:4829 (2021), which lists "light aberration, refraction, zenith attraction, diurnal aberration, and atmospheric extinction". I used this rather than Ceplecha 1987 as the finding suggested, because I could fetch and quote it; Ceplecha 1987 is behind an ADS abstract I could not verify the wording of, and the sourcing standard wants a public source I have actually read.

FINDING 7. Applied the first branch: the scope condition now opens the compression note, so the first words under render.py's "The list overstates its own source" heading say this is the nearest located text and not a demonstrated source, and name that the cluster credits no originator. drifted=True kept — the content difference is real and worth publishing. The second branch (changing the render heading) is an operator/render.py decision and is in record_problems.

record_problems.argument:
All nine findings were checked against the primary source rather than against the finding text. I pulled the Internet Archive scan of Bouw, GEOCENTRICITY: CHRISTIANITY IN THE WOODSHED (2013) — GEOCENTRICITY_djvu.xml plus GEOCENTRICITY_page_numbers.json — and rebuilt a leaf→printed-page index instead of trusting the flat djvu text. The convention in this book is a running head at the TOP of each leaf (verso "556 Chapter 36", recto "Lesser Evidences 555"), and the leaf/printed offset is a stable +17 through the body and +16 in the appendices; I confirmed it against nine independent anchors (pp. 3, 4, 5, 15, 92-note, 104, 425, 473, 534). On that index, eight of nine findings were confirmed on the page and applied to scripts/_b10_R11.py. The ninth (the clusters.py basis line) I confirmed as a real defect but did not touch, because clusters.py is not my file; it is reported upward with the page evidence and a proposed replacement.

Two of the applied fixes I deliberately did not implement in the exact form proposed, both because the proposal would have introduced a fresh error of the class it was fixing. (1) The Miller fix proposed calling him "the last credentialed physicist to press it" — that is an unscoped superlative of exactly the kind finding (i) is about, and it is probably false: Reginald Cahill (Flinders University) published absolute-motion-detection claims built on Miller's data in the 2000s. I named Miller as the exception the movement itself cites and scoped the 1905 claim to the mainstream, without the superlative. (2) The p. 4 elision fix proposed restoring the cut clause inside square brackets. Square brackets denote editorial insertion; using them here would present Bouw's own words as ours, which is a quote-integrity defect introduced while fixing a quote-integrity defect. I restored the clause plainly in both the gloss and compression.source_wording and added an explicit sentence naming that it sits inside the same sentence, that it was elided in an earlier draft, and that it cuts against us.

Verified in the source, page by page: the Sagnac sidereal-day sentence is on leaf 539 = printed 522, and the "Geocentricity predicts…" passage is on leaf 540, whose top running head reads "Rotation 523" — so the entry was attributing two quotes a page apart to one page. The Milky-Way/Scripture concession is the closing paragraph of chapter 36 on leaf 573, running head "556 Chapter 36" — p. 556, not 555. Appendix E does not stop at eq. 11: p. 746 continues "Of course, equation (11) is kinematic, not dynamic… all we have to do is to multiply both sides by the star's mass, m", producing F = ma (eq. 12), then applies it to sun, moon, planets, artificial satellites, stars and light; and the appendix opens at pp. 740–741 with the m/m "sleight of hand" argument, which was Bouw's pre-emptive answer to §3 and went unanswered. Chapter 36 note 2 attaches to the p. 534 Ellis quote ("assumed for a priori reasons and not tested by observation"), not to the abstract's equivalence result — chapter 36's note 1 is the Rubin epigraph, note 2 is the next citation, which is that quote. And p. 539 carries the hedge that was missing entirely: Ellis's model is "an oddity among cosmological models, and it is not without its problems; but it is interesting to see that the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model" — a claim that the evidence decides, which is nearer the opposite of item 310 and is stronger for our verdict than anything the entry had. Item 100 of the corpus is indeed "Miller aether drift detections."; item 293/310/318 confirmed. The Alnes & Amarzguioui abstract does say "within a radius of 15 Mpc from the center". The Springer record page for Ellis 1978 (10.1007/BF00760145) carries no retraction, erratum or correction, so the scoped replacement for "never retracted" is a claim I actually checked rather than a reworded guess.

None of this touches the verdict. SELF-CONTRADICTED rests on the contradiction being inside the book — a model asserted as making predictions that experiments confirm (pp. 3, 4, 522–523, 539, 556) alongside the Appendix E claim that dynamical arguments prove nothing either way — and the p. 539 material I added strengthens that, it does not weaken it. What is now hedged is provenance, not verdict: the entry publishes that the doctrine is Bouw's in print but not established as Bouw's in origin.
record_problems.problem: scripts/clusters.py, R11 `note` (the basis line beside the verdict chip) — CONFIRMED DEFECT, NOT MINE TO FIX. It reads: "Bouw — the movement's only credentialed astronomer — conceded his model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism and must therefore be chosen on theological grounds. That concession removes the list's own claim to be scientific evidence." That states as Bouw's settled position one horn of the contradiction the entry exists to expose, and the entry's §3 says the opposite. Source evidence, all verified on the scan: p. 3 'every fundamental experiment ever devised to measure the speed of the earth through space measures a speed of zero'; p. 4 'That evidence is so overwhelming that some physicists have concluded that physics conspires…'; p. 523 'Geocentricity predicts that earth's lack of motion is absolute… And that is exactly what fundamental experiments detect'; p. 539 'the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model'; p. 556 the chapter-36 phenomena 'point to a geocentric universe'. The theological move is real but narrow — the Earth-versus-Milky-Way residual at p. 556 and the Bible-believer sufficiency claim at p. 15 — and the note generalises it into his whole position. Suggested replacement, both horns: "Bouw states the symmetry himself — dynamical proofs 'are not proofs of anything; nor are they proofs against the geocentric universe' — and elsewhere in the same book calls the geocentric evidence overwhelming and reports his model as making predictions that experiments confirm. The list files the first claim as a proof while spending the second. Where the astronomical evidence runs out, at the Earth-versus-Galaxy gap, he names Scripture as what closes it."

per_unit.argument:
Six of the seven findings landed in my file and all six were applied, but two of them needed their proposed replacement text changed before it was safe to publish — in both cases the fix as written would have introduced a fresh error of the same class it was correcting.

Verification was done against sources, not against the findings. I read the archive.org OCR of Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I directly (/home/claude/.work/gww1.txt) and established the page-marker convention from the 384-388 run: markers sit at the FOOT of their page, after the footnote block and before the next page's running head. That confirmed footnote 752 ("It is precisely the rotation of the ether every 24 hours that accounts for the small positive results of all the interferometer experiments at the surface of the Earth") is at the foot of printed p. 387, i.e. inside the very pages the compression note said contained no rotation claim — finding 6 is right. The same convention showed the "20 km/sec" division sentence is on p. 387, not p. 386 as the gloss and the docstring both said; that is a defect nobody raised and I fixed it.

I also recovered a full text of Swenson's The Ethereal Aether (1972) and read pp. 220-226. Finding 5's truncation is real: Swenson's sentence runs "...reported that nothing was observed within one-fiftieth of the expected shift, based on Sternberg's estimate of the solar system's resultant velocity of about three thousand kilometers per second", and we cut at "expected shift". Restored, with an ellipsis-free full quotation. But I did NOT adopt the finding's conclusion that Múnera's 42.4 km/s "rests on a basis Swenson's account does not support". Swenson names Gustaf Strömberg at p. 221 as the astronomer who set the observing schedule with Miller, so his "Sternberg" is a spelling slip; and 300/sqrt(50) = 42.4 is exactly Múnera's figure, which makes "three thousand" a plausible slip of Swenson's own. Adjudicating between two secondary accounts when neither 1929 printing was reached is precisely the move this project convicts its subject of. The published text now states that the two accounts attach different bases, says neither printing was reached, and says nothing on the page turns on which is right.

Finding 1 is the most serious and is correct: our answer to our own KERNEL asserted that "the entrainment hypothesis got its altitude and its independent replication, and neither produced Miller's signal", and no result from the 1930 mountain installation is reported in Swenson's account of it. But the finding's replacement wording implies Swenson's note 29 bears on the mountain data, and it does not — the Gale-Adams correspondence is January 1930, the move was summer 1930. The concession now names the loose end first, cites note 29 as context rather than as an outcome, and rests the answer on Joos (Swenson p. 226: the Jena instrument was built in direct response to Miller's 1925 announcement and reported in September 1930 after a year's running). I flagged the January/summer trap in the docstring so a future editor cannot re-collapse it.

Finding 4's arithmetic checks out: (3100/c)^2 = 1.07e-10, so the gain to 1e-18 is eight orders, not fifteen — the old figure was comparing a fringe shift with a fractional anisotropy. Finding 7 checks out too: I fetched the EPJC 2022 paper and it mentions neither VLBI nor length-of-day, and calls its diurnal-polar-motion corrections preliminary. Rather than merely narrowing, I split the claim across three citations that actually carry it.

Finding 2 is about clusters.py, which I do not own; it is in record_problems with exact replacement text and an anchor instruction, and the docstring now carries the same, upgraded from a passing mention to an operator-actionable block.

The verdict is untouched and remains defensible: nothing I changed bears on STANDARD PHYSICS or on the filed SELF-CONTRADICTED challenge, both of which turn on the p. 387 "showed an ether drift" sentence, which I re-verified verbatim in the OCR.

changes.what_changed: Removed the unsourceable claim that the mountain installation produced a null. The concession now reads: the instrument was transported up the mountain in summer 1930 into the base of the 100-inch, the elevation Miller asked for though not the open air; NO RESULT FROM THAT INSTALLATION IS REPORTED in Swenson's account of it; his note on the same page records January 1930 correspondence indicating Michelson had by then lost interest and the latest data was 'not suitable for publication'; so the mountain run is not available to be quoted against Miller and this page does not quote it. The answer now rests on Joos: the automated 21-metre Zeiss interferometer at Jena, built in direct response to Miller's 1925 announcement, reported September 1930 after a year's running, bounding any effect below a thousandth of a fringe and any aether wind under 1.5 km/s. Final sentence changed from 'got its altitude and its independent replication' to 'got its independent replication at full instrumental strength'.
changes.evidence: Swenson p. 225, read in full text: 'notwithstanding the fact that the elaborate interferometer in Pasadena had shown no displacements worthy of notice, in the summer of 1930 Pease and Pearson had Michelson's tremendous instrument transported up the mountain and installed in the base of the one hundred-inch telescope... it was at least at the right elevation'. per_unit.argument:
I verified every finding against the primary sources rather than against the finding text, then applied eight of the ten and rejected two proposed replacements that would have introduced fresh errors of the class they were fixing.

PAGE NUMBERS (finding 1) — CONFIRMED IN FULL, from the scan the entry names. I pulled archive.org item GallileoWasWrong's djvu.xml and page_numbers.json, rebuilt per-leaf text, and read the footers off the leaves themselves. The printed marker sits at the FOOT of its own leaf in this scan (leaf = printed page + 12 throughout the region checked), so the number under a block of text is that text's page. Leaf 722 carries the chapter head "Chapter 12 / Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentric Cosmology / By Dr. Robert Bennett" AND the geokinetic-claims list AND the footer 710 — the chapter opens on p. 710, not 709. Leaf 723 (footer 711) carries "Claims and Responses ... Response: All the various effects noted above depend on the assumption..." and, a few lines later, the Barbour-Bertotti shell passage. Russell leaf 61 = 49; the clipped Mach "no Foucault's experiment, and so on...440" and "not that a rotation of the Earth is the force" are consecutive paragraphs on ONE leaf, 216 = p. 204; Mach in full with "I prefer the second way" leaf 472 = 460; Einstein n. 492 citing "Annalen der Physik, 35, 903f" leaf 251 = 239 (correct as recorded); satellite-photograph parenthesis leaf 711 = 699; WGS84 1/298.257223563 leaf 1040 = 1028. All seven renumbered; 204 and 239 kept.

THE READING FRAME MATTERS MORE THAN THE PAGE (findings 1, 3, 8). The p. 710 sentence sits inside "there are three geokinetic claims for terrestrial motion" / "All claims center on the inertial forces ... based on the presumption of Earth's rotation" — it is the opponent's case as Bennett states it before answering. compression.source_wording carried it unlabelled as the source's own wording, which is our own hedge offence committed in our favour; it is now labelled and quoted through the Response at p. 711. And the unscoped "Neither of them asserts items 180 or 257" was refuted by the entry's own next two paragraphs: it is now scoped to the pages read, with both near-counter-instances named.

TWO REJECTIONS. The cross-reference fix proposed ARG-B07; B07 is "Refraction is invoked ad hoc", whose Britannica use is the one-seventh refraction coefficient. The cluster whose record note reads verbatim "He quoted the correction and then denied the thing it corrects for", with real_source="Encyclopaedia Britannica article 'Levelling'" and verdict SELF-CONTRADICTED, is B06. B05 (the finding's target) was indeed wrong — Carpenter's canals — but B07 would have been a second wrong anchor. Anchored to B06. And the Noad-fraction fix proposed ⅑, which is U+2151 ⅑ ONE NINTH, not ⅟ (U+215F = ⅟) — that would have printed "⅑5000th" in place of "⅓5000th". Used the finding's safe alternative, "1/5000th part", verified against Gutenberg #69892: "a change of temperature equal to 30° Fah. will alter its length ¹⁄₅₀₀₀th part".

ARITHMETIC. The 170 does not follow and 197 does: 577:875 gives (875−577)/875 = 0.3406 against Huygens's 1/578 = 0.001730, ratio 196.9; the entry now states the quantity and the arithmetic. Peru: Rowbotham's "56,653 toises" against the 1911 Britannica's Peruvian arc of 176,945 toises over 3° 7′ 3″ = 56,760/degree, ~10 toises of equator reduction, so he is ~100 toises low — and his own text supports "did not survive scrutiny" only for Lapland, where he prints the Swedish verdict "196 toises more than the true length". Air density: I did not adopt the finding's factor of ~150, because Rowbotham's authority is Derham's air-pump result, which he quotes at "two seconds in an hour" — 5.6e-4 in period, 1.1e-3 on seconds-pendulum length, and 18% of that for his own 84.2/0 °F range gives 0.02% against 0.436%, a factor of ~20. That is the most generous reading available to him and it is the one now published as the headline, with the buoyancy-plus-added-mass calculation (~1e2) beside it; the steelman's and §7's "several hundred" are corrected to match.

The REFUTED verdict is untouched and survives: it rests on ch. 4 p. 204, ch. 1 p. 49 and ch. 5 p. 239, none of which moved in substance.

per_unit.argument:
All eight findings pointed at real defects in scripts/_b11_A16.py and all eight are now fixed. Two of the eight, however, carried proposed replacement text that was itself wrong on the facts, and in both cases I substituted a source-verified version rather than the one offered — the same class of error the finding was correcting.

WHAT I VERIFIED, AND HOW.
- Rowbotham 1865, Project Gutenberg #69892 (pg69892.txt, fetched fresh): "balloon" occurs THIRTEEN times, at lines 424, 441, 444, 452, 468, 473, 483, 488, 491, 503, 510, 1793, 2900 — exactly the lines the finding names. The entry's "six" was wrong. But the finding's proposed replacement says "ten in one section on the apparent concavity"; the run at lines 424-510 is ELEVEN occurrences. I published eleven. Line 1793 is confirmed as Section 7, "Cause of 'Sunrise' and 'Sunset'", where Rowbotham attributes apparent descent to "a simple and everywhere visible law of perspective" and illustrates it with a balloon — genuinely the strongest thing available for section 3, and now used there.
- Dubay proof 22 (Internet Archive djvu OCR, /home/claude/dubay200.txt line 300): "spending 3 hours ascending over New Mexico". The entry put 2.5 h in his mouth and then reverse-engineered his 2,500 miles from a duration he never gave. Confirmed and fixed.
- Dubay proof 158 (line 2091-2099): confirmed verbatim, and confirmed that it grants co-rotation arguendo and predicts EASTWARD sweeping. Our §2 was reporting observed eastward drift as if it refuted the cluster; against proofs 21/22 it does, against 158 it concedes. This was the most serious of the eight and the body now answers 158 explicitly.
- Wikipedia Radiosonde (wikitext fetched): "Because a sonde may drift several hundred kilometers during the 90- to 120-minute flight, there may be concern that this could introduce problems into the model initialization. However, this appears not to be so except perpaps locally in jet stream regions in the stratosphere." [sic "perhaps"]. We had dropped the negation and three hedges in our own favour. This is the hedge rule violated on our side and is now corrected in the refutation, the sources[] label and the docstring.
- Carpenter 1885, Gutenberg #55387: proof 44 "the Earth is said to move at the rate of nineteen miles in a second of time, 'from west to east'"; proof 49 "revolving through space from west to east at the rate of nineteen miles in a second". Confirmed — he welds the orbital magnitude to a rotational direction and draws no distinction. Our "aimed at the Earth's revolution around the Sun / answering different motions" invented precision the source does not have.
- Arithmetic reproduced: u = Omega cos(phi) [R^2/(R+z) - (R+z)] = -4.731 m/s at 33.4 N, z = 38,969 m; 42.6 km over 2.5 h. Against 2,169 mi (3,491 km) that is a factor of 82.0 — under two orders, not three. Confirmed. Also computed Omega*z*cos(phi) = 2.37 m/s for the new proof-158 paragraph.

VERDICT UNAFFECTED. Nothing here touches the REFUTED challenge; if anything the 158 answer strengthens it, because it closes the one place where a defender could have said we reported his prediction as our refutation. clusters.py untouched, as are deep.py, people.py, works.py, render.py, build.py, tests/ and review/corrections.json.

per_unit.argument:
I own scripts/_b10_A19.py only. I verified every finding against the primary scans rather than against the finding text, and all seven held; I applied all seven, correcting two places where the finding's own proposed replacement was imprecise.

METHOD. I pulled the two archive.org OCRs the entry names — item GallileoWasWrong (Vol. I, 3,335,538 bytes) and item GalileoWasWrongTheChurchSungenisRobertA.Bennett4276 (Vol. II, 1,771,293 bytes) — and normalised whitespace, since the OCR double-spaces words and has no form-feed page breaks. Before touching a single citation I established the page-marker convention from three independent anchors rather than assuming the finding was right: (i) the printed folio sits at the FOOT of its page, immediately before the running head of the next ("709 / Chapter 12 / Galileo Was Wrong"), so text between markers N and N+1 is page N+1; (ii) the volume's own contents page lists "Physical Constituents of a Geocentric Universe 715" and that section lands exactly where the convention puts it; (iii) the contents page lists "Michelson-Gale: Claims and Responses 745" and the text beginning "Michelson-Gale:" lands on that page under the same convention, with the Claims and Responses one page further on. Three anchors agreeing, in a scan where the entry had every folio one too low.

FINDING 1 (major, page numbers) CONFIRMED IN FULL. Corrected values, each located by offset between markers: geokinetic list 709→710, Claim #1 response and "Implicitly denied" 710→711, "No measurement of absolute or preferred rotation" 711→712, Sagnac points 15-16 741→742, Michelson-Gale response point 3 745→746, Eddington-via-Sciama footnote 615 310→311. The finding's 745/746 split is also right and I verified it directly: p. 745 ENDS with "The Sagnac time difference is: At = 4Aco/c2", and the latitude geometry plus the sinφ form OPEN p. 746. All quoted sentences were verbatim-correct; only locations moved. I fixed the docstring, locator, gloss, straw_man, compression.note and sources[0].

I also found a defect the finding did not name: the locator and docstring gave Vol. I ch. 12 the title "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism". That is Vol. II ch. 10's title. Vol. I ch. 12 is "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentric Cosmology" — confirmed at both the chapter head and the contents page. Fixed.

On the Vol. II range I did not simply copy the finding's "157-159". The contents page reads "Chapter 10 Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism 157", and the markers put the geokinetic claim and the "Implicitly denied" response on p. 158 and "No measurement..." on p. 159. I wrote it as "opens at p. 157; the claim and the Mach response at pp. 158-159", which is what the scan supports.

FINDING 2 (major, straw man attributes a claim the source does not make) CONFIRMED. I read the whole of p. 711. The book's Response is to its own Claim #1 — the popular geokinetic argument — not to the physics literature, and two paragraphs later on that same page it cites the computation approvingly: "Barbour and Bertotti proved that a large hollow sphere (representing the distant star fields) rotating around a small solid sphere inside ... produced exactly the same pattern of Coriolis and centrifugal forces". The Vol. II contents page carries "Brill and Cohen's Geocentrism 142", "Lynden-Bell's Geocentrism 146", "Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism 147". And our own gloss quotes Eddington, via Sciama, via the book's footnote 615, denying exactly the Machian alternative from inside the literature. So "the alternative is not denied in the literature; it is computed in it" was contradicted three ways, including by our own entry. Withdrawn. I published the narrower charge the finding suggested — that the word "implicitly" understates a rejection that was explicit and quantitative, and that the Claim #1 response does not meet it at the point where it deploys the phrase — with the book given its due on the Barbour-Bertotti citation, and scoped ("at the point where it deploys the phrase", not "nowhere in the book").

FINDING 3 (moderate, markup in an escaped field) CONFIRMED. render.py line 242 emits straw_man.detail through e(). I checked all 63 treatment files: A19 was the only one writing tags into it. Rewritten as plain text with literal typographic characters; the ARG-R01 pointer is now bare text pointing at the Related line the renderer prints directly below.

FINDING 4 (moderate, quadrature) CONFIRMED. sqrt((Ω sinφ)² + (Ω cosφ sin Az)²) = Ω only when |sin Az| = 1, and the entry's own next sentence — a north-aimed gyro at the equator "holds still against both the sky and the ground at once" — already contradicted the quadrature sentence. Rewritten to state it of the field, not the readings, and I applied the same correction to advocate.preemptive (2), which rests the whole answer to the ether-vortex move on that constraint and carried the same conflation.

FINDING 5 (moderate, plumb line vs geometric normal) CONFIRMED as a real gap. Named the assumption in section 3 and in steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, and closed the escape on cost. I scoped the reversal leg more tightly than the finding did: the Foucault sign argument holds for rotation about the axis through the disc centre — which is what every flat cosmology proposes, the stars wheeling about Polaris — because Ω·n̂ is Ω cos(plumb tilt) and a tilt under a right angle cannot make a cosine negative. An unscoped version would fail for an axis lying in the plane, so I did not write one.

FINDING 6 (moderate, hedge rule on our own side) CONFIRMED. source_wording now carries the unhedged p. 746 sentence alongside the hedged ones. The 60-word cap bites: the three sentences in full run 94 words. I quoted 55 — the geokinetic claim entire (18), the "No measurement ... has not been disproven experimentally" hedge elided to 17 with ellipses, and the p. 746 sentence's leading clause through "relative to the rotating heavens" (20) — and completed the sentence in our own prose rather than truncating silently. compression.note now states why force_upgraded survives: the flat statement is made of FREE instruments, a pendulum and a light ring, while item 229 asserts it of the gyrocompass, the one instrument built by gravity control and damping to stop being free.

FINDING 7 (moderate, item 224) CONFIRMED. Item 224 is "No rotation proof mechanical." — four words that in the geocentric idiom read as this page's own first-paragraph concession, and the entry asserted the other reading without argument. I published the dilemma and moved the verdict's weight onto item 12 against 225/229, which does not depend on how 224 is read. The verdict stays defensible on that leg alone, so no verdict challenge.

Nothing else was touched. No tests, no build, no git. python3 -c "import ast; ast.parse(...)" passes on my file and the ENTRY dict execs cleanly with all eleven keys intact.

per_unit.argument:
All seven findings were checked against the primary texts on disk (archive.org enlarged-edition OCR `za3e.txt`/`ZeteticAstronomy-EarthNotaGlobe-3e-format2_djvu.txt`, Gutenberg 69892 for 1865, Gutenberg 55387 for Carpenter, two Dubay OCRs) rather than against the finding text, and all seven were substantially right. Four sub-claims inside them were wrong and were corrected rather than copied in, which is where most of the work went.

The two majors were the serious ones and both were the project's own convict-class defect pointed inward. (1) Section 5 called Carpenter's proof 32 "the cleanest single check on this page" because 6 ft at 3 miles reproduces sqrt(2Rh). It equally reproduces the zetetic tradition's own law: Parallax quotes Mayhew's Wonders of Science p. 357 at enlarged-ed. p. 160 — "when an object is removed from the eye 3000 times its own diameter, it will only just be distinguishable" — and adopts it ("The above may be called the law of perspective."). 3000 x 6 ft = 3.41 mi against the sphere's 3.00 mi, and the two laws cross at h = 2R/9e6 = 1.42 m, i.e. just under the six feet Carpenter names. The page was making its cleanest check at the one height where the rival predictions agree. Worse, the closing sentence said the perspective account "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever" — flatly contradicted three lines above in Carpenter's own proof 6 ("no matter how high we ascend above the level of the sea, the horizon rises on and still on as we rise"; Federal Hill, Baltimore, twenty-five miles) and in Rowbotham's proposition 2 and his "at a certain distance, less or greater, according to the elevation of the observer". Section 5 is rewritten: proof 32 demoted and explicitly labelled non-discriminating, proof 6 promoted, their law stated as linear in height against the sphere's square root, with the fifteen-thousand-mile figure and a non-circular check I added (their rule run backwards needs an eye only 352 ft up for a 200-mile horizon).

(2) Our headline internal-contradiction argument — his optics exempt the axis his own tilt-to-contact procedure uses — was published as an oversight of his while his printed answer to exactly that charge sat two sentences past the sentence we quote. He writes that the dip taken this way is the geometric angle "to which must be added the collimation", "always A, T, S, plus collimation", because "the spider's web of which the cross hair is made is placed in the actual centre; hence, in an observation, the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it". That is now in refutation 2(a), in the steelman's first reply, and in the gloss (which previously located his answer in the 1865 text only, telling a reader of the edition we quote that his reply lived elsewhere). The TLDR, which stated the exemption flat with no hedge at all, now says the defect acts off the axis and his procedure puts the horizon on it, "though he saw that objection and answered it in the same section" — and the weight is moved to the square-root scaling, which is what the body actually holds. The verdict survives: (c) never depended on (a), and demoting (a) from kill to pressure point strengthens rather than weakens the rejection of SELF-CONTRADICTED, so I updated both places that gave the rejection reasoning.

The four moderates were applied with corrections. The "10-to-17-mile ranges his text names" was a number in quotation-adjacent position that neither text carries (Experiment 7 says "a length of ten to twenty miles" and "Ten miles on each side"; Dubay 60 says "a clear, flat 10-20 miles"; the only "17 miles" in the enlarged edition is an Australian latitude discrepancy) — fixed to ten-to-twenty and 2.2-4.3 arcmin, in the refutation, in straw_man.detail where the same figure appeared, in the advocate's paraphrase of it, and in docstring note 5. The unscoped absence assertion about the 1849 pamphlet is now scoped and no longer waves away a 16-page text whose own title advertises sea-surface experiments. "A plane does not look like a bowl" is replaced with his actual theory of why a plane would look like a bowl — the amphitheatre/concavity passage two paragraphs before the balloon quotations and the long-room/tunnel analogy immediately after them. The collimation-definition problem in the reversal test is real and I fixed it, but not the way the finding proposed (see rejected). Docstring note 11(e) is a false report-up and is withdrawn in place.

Three further defects of the same classes turned up while verifying and were fixed: docstring note 2 had the two-face argument backwards ("[the residual] cannot reverse sign under transit" — it is precisely the residual that reverses); the gloss said Elliott "opens by conceding the point at issue" when he opens by saying the opposite and concedes in the next sentence, and it silently italicised "Philosophy imposes the truth upon us" in a quotation that carries no italics in the source; and a quoted phrase was truncated at "the several glasses" without an ellipsis, now quoted through "of the theodolite".

The two that mattered most were both cases of the project's own house offence pointed inward: a quoted string attributed to a source that does not contain it (the "nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" phrase is Andrew Young's, not the USNO's — I confirmed the USNO page verbatim, "obtained by adding the average apparent radius of the Sun (16 arcminutes) to the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)", and Young's page verbatim, "the sum of an average radius of 16 minutes, and a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes"), and a Dubay quotation stopped at the concession with the flat conclusion that finishes the same sentence dropped ("…unlike a hazy illusory mirage, and on a ball-Earth 25,000 miles in circumference should be 2,400 feet below the horizon", verified at flatearth.ws/eric-dubay). One place I refined rather than followed the finding: finding 3's proposed replacement collapsed the comparison to two cases and would have discarded the EXPERIMENT 3 three-mile figure the entry already had right, so I kept three yardsticks and attached the factors separately (roughly 240 at six miles, roughly 250 at three, order a hundred against the "several feet" of the 1870 trial) rather than adopting its wording wholesale.

All seven findings were checked against the primary texts before anything was edited; six were confirmed and applied in scripts/_b11_B10.py, and the seventh (the clusters.py record) is correct but sits outside the one file I own, so it goes to record_problems with an anchoring instruction rather than being applied.

The headline defect was real and was ours. Carpenter's proof 89 (Gutenberg #55387, lines 1342-1371 of the local carpenter100.txt) reads: "It is well known that the law regulating the apparent decrease in the size of objects ... is very different with luminous bodies ... Sail past the light of a small lamp in a row-boat on a dark night, and it will seem to be no smaller when a mile off than it was when close to it. Proctor says, in speaking of the Sun: 'his apparent size does not change,'--far off or near. And then he forgets the fact!" Carpenter asserts the law himself, in his own voice, with his own example, and endorses Proctor's line as "the fact". The entry's through-line - TLDR "the words are a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against", the §3 heading "is Proctor's sentence, borrowed", and compression.note "Nothing was misquoted; the speech act moved" - flattered our own provenance finding by relocating the movement's own claim onto an opponent, and it did so while our own source_wording field quoted "And then he forgets the fact!" unanalysed. force_upgraded ("a concession was re-used as a proof") cannot describe the Carpenter-to-list step, because proof 89 was already a numbered proof; the concession-to-proof move, if it happened anywhere, happened in 1885. Refiled as hedge_dropped, with the note saying openly that no enum value fits exactly and naming what the fragment actually strips: that the law is about how luminous bodies appear, that it is asserted to deny an inference, and that the paragraph ends by calling Proctor's objection a counterfeit rather than by reporting a measurement.

Three other confirmations. (a) Dubay #123 credits the 32-mile figure to "Flat-Earthers throughout the ages" and #147 cites nobody; the only naming of Zetetic Cosmogony located in the archive.org text of 200 Proofs is #31, which is the kite-flying/wind passage - matching the project doc's named-source map "Winship -> 31". "Documented at every link" was indefensible and is gone. (b) In the Winship scan, "We challenge the whole scientific world to disprove this statement," closes the sun's-DISTANCE argument at line 7812, immediately before the section heading "SUN'S DIAMETER." at 7816; the units error's own challenge is "Let him disprove this who can. If ever disproof is attempted, it will be a literary curiosity, well worth framing." at 7890-7896. The entry had the quote on the wrong claim while its own sources[] label placed it correctly - a self-contradiction inside one record. (c) The §6 "reverses it" was overstated and Rowbotham 1865 Section 8 supplies the defence: it already carries the whole mechanism ("as the air near the Earth is both more dense and more damp ... the light of the Sun must be dilated or enlarged as well as modified in colour") and only then subordinates it with "But the enlarged appearance ... is only an optical impression, as proved by actual measurement" plus Philips. 1881 chapter X keeps the identical mechanism ("the disc of light projected upon the atmosphere", verified via the served za28) and drops the concession, promoting the residue to "a striking argument against the rotundity of the earth". Recast as the edition diff, which is true, stronger, and survives the glare-versus-disc reply.

One incidental verification worth recording: I established the Winship scan's page-marker convention rather than assuming it, because the p. 120 citation is load-bearing (Scott 1901 gives the same page). The markers sit at the HEAD of their page - text following marker N is page N. Anchors: the contents list pages "Sun, The" 112, "Sun's Distance" 113, "Sun's Diameter" 119, "Stars, The" 120; the tightest test is the body heading "THE STARS" falling between markers 120 (line 7864) and 121 (line 7927), which the contents puts on 120. Under the foot convention it would be 121. So the sextant derivation is on printed p. 120 and the locator's "pp. 119-120" is correct as published.

The verdict is untouched and remains defensible. Nothing applied moves MISLEADING: finding 1 makes Carpenter's commitment to constancy stronger, not weaker, which if anything hardens the case against the fragment; the equal-size half still rests on an observation true in every model, and the constancy half is still true on one timescale and false on another.

per_unit.argument:
Six of the seven findings survived checking and are applied to scripts/_b10_B11.py; one is rejected with evidence from the page's own rendered verdict legend.

CONFIRMED AND FIXED. (1) The precedent cite was genuinely wrong: clusters.py:486-488 gives C09 the verdict UNFALSIFIABLE ("Devotional imagery is not survey data"), and scripts/_b9_C09.py:303 only *proposes* SELF-CONTRADICTED. Citing a pending proposal as settled precedent, in a rendered field, on a provenance page, is exactly the slip the finding names. (2) The ducting physics was wrong in our favour's opposite direction — k = 1/(1 + R dn/dh) goes to infinity at dN/dh = -157 N-units/km, so a duct is not "a larger k"; and the correct treatment (modified refractivity M = N + (h/R_e)x10^6 ~ N + 0.157h, with 0.157 per metre = 10^6/R) puts 1/R inside the very formalism used to compute ducted propagation on a flat grid, which is section 5's thesis arriving from the least convenient direction. Two sources added for it. (3) The bathymetry numbers really were two models chained as one: 1.0 m is 1% of depth (range scaling, no bending), 7.26 m is the pure-bending across-track shift holding depth, and the honest combined figure is about 3.5 m across-track and about 2.1 m in depth (about 1.9 m the other way for the opposite-sign bias). Each is now attached to its mechanism; the vertical term went UP, so the conclusion strengthens. (4) The unscoped SAR universal, the NWS label's two dropped hedges plus the grafted 60 nm figure (source wording verified by fetch: "often produces the largest errors, usually causing precipitation underestimation", and the 60 nm/124 nm POD drop belongs to a separate sentence attributing it to Kitchen and Jackson 1993).

REJECTED. Finding 2 asks us to demote the SELF-CONTRADICTED challenge to REFUTED on the ground that "one item whose named technique falsifies it" is not how this page uses the verdict. The page's own published legend (scripts/render.py:635-637) reads: "SELF-CONTRADICTED - the claim's own source, or another item on the same list, points the other way." That is two branches, and both are in use. The intra-item branch is A19 (clusters.py:172-175), which has no originator, no source and no second item: the verdict rests entirely on the named instrument, "a gyrocompass finds true north by sensing Earth's rotation" - structurally identical to item 392's flat-earth phase. B06 is the same branch via the claimant's own source. The second half of the objection - that leaning on item 391 spends an item scored at R08 twice - fails on the legend's wording "another item on the same LIST", and on precedent: C10's counterpart is C03 and B13's is B07, both cross-cluster. Adopting the proposed fix would have replaced a correct verdict argument with one that mis-describes our own rubric - the same class of error the finding was aimed at. per_unit.argument:
All five findings against D09 were checked against the primary files, not against the finding text, and all five turned out to name a real defect. Two of them I could do better than the proposed fix, and one of the proposed replacements would have introduced a fresh bibliographic error of exactly the class it was correcting.

Finding 1 (Kepler/Galileo) — CONFIRMED at source. I re-downloaded the exact djvu.txt the entry links (archive.org GalileoWasWrongTheChurchSungenisRobertA.Bennett4276, 1,771,293 bytes). "astrolog" returns exactly two hits: line 31273, "Without them Kepler would have been just another seventeenth-century astronomer struggling to make a living by reading astrological horoscopes" (the "them" being Brahe's charts and data), and line 31539, "Having previously dabbled in astrology, Galileo wrote a personal horoscope for Cosimo Medici". The entry described both as being about Galileo. Fixed in the gloss, in the sources[] label and in docstring note 4b, with the Kepler hit quoted so the error cannot be made again silently.

Finding 2 (unnamed scope of three searches) — CONFIRMED, and I widened the search rather than only narrowing the claim. The GWW file's own first page reads "Vol[ume] II / Chapters 7 to 13 / Seventh edition / ... 2013"; PG #69892's metadata and title page both give Simpkin, Marshall, 1865; PG #55387's title page gives "1885 ... 5th Edition: 6th Thousand". All three are now named in the gloss and in their labels. Beyond that, I located and searched the enlarged 1881 THIRD edition (archive.org zeteticastronomy-earthnotaglobe, file ZeteticAstronomy-EarthNotaGlobe-3e-format2_djvu.txt — title page "1881", and it carries the Sabine pendulum material that only the third edition has) and Dubay's 200 Proofs: "astrol", "zodia" and "horoscop" all return zero hits in both, as they do in the 1865 text and in Carpenter. So the zetetic-side absence is now established over four texts including the edition the movement actually circulates, not one.

Finding 3 (generalisation from three files to two lineages) — CONFIRMED. "Neither cosmological lineage brought this argument in" and docstring "The founding flat-earth texts have no astrology argument in them" are both unscoped absence claims. Both now read "in the texts searched", with what was NOT searched named in the body: Rowbotham's 1873 second edition, Volumes I and III of Galileo Was Wrong, and (in the docstring) Blount, Voliva, Johnson, Bouw, van der Kamp, Marshall Hall.

Finding 4 (leg 2 of the verdict challenge) — CONFIRMED on both counts. The punchline clause "and that occultist is a heliocentrist" is an attribution to Manly P. Hall, which the same paragraph says is not established, so "it needs no attribution at all" was false as written; and the defender's reply is decisive — D10's thesis is that heliocentrism has occult roots, so an occultist heliocentrist confirms D10 rather than contradicting it. "Either leg alone carries the verdict" and "needs no attribution at all" are struck; leg 2 is now explicitly "SUPPORTING ONLY" with both limits stated; refutation §5 restates the residue as an inconsistency of standing rather than a contradiction; the reply is added to advocate.best_defense as a fifth move and answered in preemptive (d), which records the concession and warns a later editor not to restore the struck sentences. survives stays at 4 and preemptive now carries four concrete changes, satisfying the deep.py rule that survives>=3 obligates a text change.

Finding 5 (three unsourced prevalence claims) — CONFIRMED. I re-read astro.com/swisseph/swephinfo_e.htm: it says the Swiss Ephemeris "is not a product for end users. It is a toolset for programmers to build into their astrological software" and that it "contains three ephemerides" — the JPL DE files, Astrodienst's compression, or Moshier's semi-analytic theory (based on DE404) — and it makes no adoption or market-share statement anywhere. All three prevalence claims are replaced by the documented version, which needs no market claim to make the same point, plus a standing instruction in note 8(d) not to reintroduce one. I also softened one further implicit prevalence claim in refutation §6 that the finding did not name.

The cluster verdict in clusters.py is untouched, as are all shared files.

The 9°/12° offset in the proposed fix also checks out (18 vs 27, 56 vs 44), so I kept the numbers and gave both radiants explicitly rather than the word "displaced".

EGAL, WIEGERT, BROWN & VIDA, ApJ (2023), arXiv:2302.02915 + published PDF. "The main peak (ZHR ~27) occurred around 69°.42 ± 0°.01 (4 hr–4 hr 30 UT) on May 31"; "We find that ordinary cometary activity could have produced other TAH apparitions observed in the past, including in 1930 and 2017"; abstract opens "The τ-Herculids (IAU shower number #61 TAH)". Findings 2 and 5 both CONFIRMED.

YE & VAUBAILLON, MNRAS Letters 515:L45 (2022), full text at ar5iv: "Increased activity of the τ-Herculid meteor shower has been observed on 2022 May 30–31 but only reached ∼1/50 of storm level". Finding 2's rate point CONFIRMED; note the arXiv landing-page abstract is the revised one and does NOT carry this sentence — it is in the paper body, which is where I got it.

REJECTED CLAUSE. Finding 2's proposed replacement says the outburst arrived "within minutes of the 2001 and 2008 timings". It did not. Our own body gives Lüthen 04:55 UT and Horii 04:59 UT; Egal puts the observed main peak at 04h–04h30 UT. That is roughly 25–55 minutes, not "minutes". Writing "within minutes" would have been the same class of defect as the "rate and width in general agreement" clause it was replacing. I wrote "inside an hour of the times set down in 2001 and 2008" and gave the observed bracket, which is still a striking result for a 21-year-ahead forecast and is checkable.

SPURNÝ, BOROVIČKA, MUCKE & SVOREŇ, A&A 605:A68 (2017), full text at ar5iv: "Asher & Clube 1993 predicted that future encounters would occur in 1995, 1998, 2005, and 2008" and, separately, "Asher & Izumi 1998 showed that enhanced Taurid activity indeed occurred in the years when the center of the swarm was less than 40° in mean anomaly from the Earth". Finding 3 CONFIRMED: a 1998 paper cannot confirm 2005 and 2008, and our source label said it did. I also found an unflagged arithmetic slip in the same sentence: the paper says "The total number of Taurid fireballs recorded photographically ... in 2015 was about 200. This is much more than we recorded in any previous year" but "For this study we selected 144 Taurids with complete information about heliocentric orbits". The 113-member branch is a subset of the 144, not of the ~200; our body implied the latter. Fixed in the same edit and recorded in the docstring.

ROBERTSON, POKORNÝ, GRANVIK, WHEELER & RUMPF, PSJ 2:88 (2021): title is "Latitude Variation of Flux and Impact Angle of Asteroid Collisions with Earth and the Moon"; models the near-Earth OBJECT population; "the flux of impacts to the poles for Earth is 22% greater than the flux at the equator, and 55% greater for the Moon". Finding 6 CONFIRMED — the figure was being deployed in verdict_challenge against a claim about micrometeoroid fallout, a population the paper does not model. I scoped it in three places (body, verdict_challenge, source label) rather than two, so the transplant cannot recur from the label.

FINDING 1, the hedge/consistency defect, is the serious one and it is real. §2 opened "prediction is the one thing a coordinate relabelling cannot manufacture" and closed "They are not compatible with the Earth being somewhere else", while §5 says in our own voice that a Tychonic relabelling "reproduces ... every annual date". The entry's own advocate.preemptive forbids exactly that, and build.py strips the advocate block, so readers saw the violated sentence and not the instruction. Both sentences replaced with claims §5 can live with. This makes the entry MORE consistent with its STANDARD PHYSICS verdict ("real, already explained, does not discriminate"), not less, so the verdict is untouched and stands.

FINDING 8. I took the "cut it" branch rather than the "argue it" branch. The proposed argument — that a moving-sky model has no mechanism to impose the observer's 0.4 km/s on meteoroids already in the atmosphere — is not obviously sound and is uncited, and by the page's own logic in that same paragraph a relabelling that absorbs 29.8 km/s absorbs 0.46 km/s too. So the diurnal-aberration fact is retained, now cited, but explicitly marked as a fact about how the working model is assembled and NOT a further discriminator, with "this page does not claim it could not" stated in our own voice. §5 still lists exactly three survivors (the third is now the spherical-Earth/Tychonic-unavailability point alone), so no count moved. advocate.preemptive clause (2) rewritten to say TWO things carry the weight, not three, and to name the earlier draft's error so it is not reintroduced.

changes.what_changed: Withdrew the claim that the Ciufolini-Pavlis observable is "the 1/a3 difference between LAGEOS and LAGEOS II". (1) of gr-qc/0412057. Finding cited "Eq. (4)" and 48.1 - eq. (4) in that paper is the older node-node-perigee combination (c1=0.304, c2=-0.350, 60.2 mas/yr), so the finding's citation was wrong while its substance was right.
